options: One cluster containing all observations, then splits it
k randomly chosen centroids
n singleton clusters (each observation is its own cluster), then merges
A pre-specified number of clusters k
questions.explanation: Agglomerative clustering is a bottom-up approach: it starts with n singleton clusters and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters until all observations are in a single cluster. Divisive hierarchical clustering is the reverse (top-down).

questions.text: Which linkage criterion is most likely to produce the 'chaining effect' (one giant cluster absorbing individuals)?
options: Ward
Complete
Average
Single
questions.explanation: Single linkage defines inter-cluster distance as the minimum pairwise distance. This means a cluster can grow by absorbing any nearby point, even if that point is far from most of the cluster — producing long, chain-like clusters.

questions.text: In a dendrogram, the HEIGHT at which two clusters merge represents:
options: The number of observations in each cluster
The inter-cluster distance at the time of the merge
The WCSS reduction achieved by the merge
The number of steps taken to reach this merge
questions.explanation: The y-axis of a dendrogram is the dissimilarity (distance) at which two clusters were merged. Merges at low height join very similar clusters; merges at high height join dissimilar clusters. This is why the final merge (all into one) is at the top.

questions.text: You run hclust on 5,000 observations and then call cutree(hc, k = 4). What does this return?
options: A dendrogram with 4 branches highlighted
An integer vector of length 5,000, giving each observation's cluster label (1–4)
A list of 4 centroids
The height at which the dendrogram is cut to give 4 clusters
questions.explanation: cutree() cuts the dendrogram at the height that yields k clusters and returns an integer vector of cluster labels — one label per observation. You can then attach this to your data frame for profiling.

questions.text: Hierarchical clustering is more scalable than k-means and is the preferred method for datasets with more than 100,000 rows.
questions.explanation: Hierarchical clustering requires computing and storing an n × n distance matrix, which is O(n²) in both time and memory. For n = 100,000, this would require storing 10 billion distances. k-means is far more scalable for large datasets.

questions.text: Ward's linkage criterion merges the two clusters that minimise which quantity?
options: The minimum pairwise distance between any two points across clusters
The maximum pairwise distance between any two points across clusters
The increase in total within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS) after the merge
The difference in cluster sizes after the merge
questions.explanation: Ward's linkage merges the pair of clusters whose combination produces the smallest increase in WCSS — exactly the k-means objective. This is why Ward tends to produce compact, similarly-sized clusters similar to those from k-means, and is usually the best default for continuous data.
